module_title: Atmospheric Pressure, Coriolis Effect, and Pressure Belts
introduction: Wind is simply air in motion. But what causes it to move? At this level, we will understand that 'differences in atmospheric pressure' drive the winds. We will also analyze the global pressure belts and how Earth's rotation curves the winds.

core_concepts.title: The Golden Rule of Wind
core_concepts.description: Wind ALWAYS blows from areas of 'High Atmospheric Pressure' to areas of 'Low Atmospheric Pressure'. High pressure is usually associated with cold, sinking air (clear skies). Low pressure is associated with warm, rising air (clouds and rain).

core_concepts.title: The Coriolis Effect (Ferrel's Law)
core_concepts.description: Because the Earth rotates from West to East, moving air (wind) does not travel in a straight line. It is deflected. Ferrel's Law states: Winds are deflected to their 'Right' in the Northern Hemisphere and to their 'Left' in the Southern Hemisphere. The Coriolis force is zero at the equator and maximum at the poles.

core_concepts.title: Equatorial Low-Pressure Belt (The Doldrums)
core_concepts.description: Located between 5°N and 5°S. Intense heating by the sun causes air to expand and rise vertically, creating a zone of low pressure. Because the air is moving upwards rather than horizontally, surface winds are extremely weak. This calm zone is called the 'Doldrums'.

core_concepts.title: Sub-Tropical High-Pressure Belt (Horse Latitudes)
core_concepts.description: Located around 30°N and 30°S. The air that rose at the equator cools and sinks down at these latitudes, creating high pressure. It is called the 'Horse Latitudes' because, historically, Spanish sailors becalmed in these windless waters would throw their horses overboard to save drinking water.

important_entities.name: Sub-Tropical High & World Deserts
important_entities.significance: Because air is descending (sinking) at the 30° latitudes, it suppresses cloud formation and rain. Consequently, most of the world's great hot deserts (Sahara, Arabian, Great Australian, Kalahari) are located exactly along this Sub-Tropical High-Pressure Belt.

trap_alerts_and_exceptions.explanation: A very common mistake: Winds are named after the direction they 'come from', NOT the direction they are going. A 'Westerly' wind comes from the West and blows toward the East. An 'Easterly' comes from the East.

mnemonics_and_tricks.explanation: Northern Hemisphere = Right deflection. Southern Hemisphere = Left deflection.

exam_strategy_tips: Assertion/Reasoning questions frequently target the 'Doldrums' (calmness due to vertical rising air) and 'Horse Latitudes' (sinking air).
Lines joining places having equal atmospheric pressure on a map are called 'Isobars'.
